title: Only two Yoshinoya branches in all of Japan are on a train platform, and this is one of them
description: Gyudon on the go in Kyobashi Station. When you spot a restaurant on a train platform in Japan, the odds are extremely high that it’s going to be a noodle joint, and specifically a soba/udon one. Since they both use the same sort of broth, the logistics of keeping a pot of it heated and […]
content:
Gyudon on the go in Kyobashi Station.

When you spot a restaurant on a train platform in Japan, the odds are extremely high that it’s going to be a noodle joint, and specifically a soba/udon one. Since they both use the same sort of broth, the logistics of keeping a pot of it heated and always having batches of noodles boiling makes it pretty easy to serve up meals in a speedy fashion.

But while he was passing through Osaka’s Kyobashi Station the other day, our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa spotted something he couldn’t recall ever seeing anywhere else: a station platform Yoshinoya.

This appears to be one of only two station platform Yoshinoya’s in all of Japan. Curious to see if it pares down its selection to just the bare-bones basics for easier operations, Seiji stepped inside and took a look at the ordering touch screen, but nope, this branch looks to offer the same full menu as other Yoshinoyas that aren’t five steps away from where commuters and travelers are getting on or off trains.

▼ Whether you want just a standard beef bowl or the deluxe, limited-time combo meal with grilled unagi (eel), stewed gyudon beef, miso soup, and a salad, the Kyobashi Station Yoshinoya’s cooks are ready to accommodate you.

OK, so they’ve got the regular menu, and also the regular Yoshinoya prices, with no extra price gouging despite the convenience of being right on the platform. But does this unconventional setup mean that the quality suffers?

Not a bit! Seiji’s beef bowl was 100-percent as delicious as the ones he’s had at regular Yoshinoya branches.

Because of all that, eating at the Kyobashi Station Yoshinoya is a surreal mix of everyday and unusual vibes. The familiar food looks, tastes, and costs the same as it would at any other Yoshinoya. But look up from your beef bowl, and you’ll see trains coming and going in front of you without having to get up from your seat at the counter.

And while all Yoshinoya branches accept payment by tapping a Suica or other prepaid train fare card, it feels like an especially appropriate way to settle your bill here.

This Yoshinoya is located on Kyobashi Station’s Osaka Loop Line outer track platform, and it’s open morning, noon, and night every day, not just during weekday rush hours. As for the only other train platform Yoshinoya in Japan, it’s on Platform 4 of Meitetsu Nagoya Station in Nagoya, a town with at least one more noteworthy platform dining option too.

title: Japanese sweet potato ice cream season! Häagen-Dazs and Muji take different paths to our hearts
description: Two completely different ways to make a delicious Japanese autumn dessert. Now that we’re into the back half of September, we’re ready to switch our sweets snacking into autumn mode. And just like how farmers are harvesting their sweet potatoes, so too is it time for us to start bringing in Japan’s sweet potato ice […]
content:
Two completely different ways to make a delicious Japanese autumn dessert.

Now that we’re into the back half of September, we’re ready to switch our sweets snacking into autumn mode. And just like how farmers are harvesting their sweet potatoes, so too is it time for us to start bringing in Japan’s sweet potato ice creams for taste testing.

Today we’re looking at two ice cream makers with very different approaches. First, we’ve got Häagen-Dazs, a premium brand that’s very comfortable with adding decadent opulence to its desserts. But we’re also trying the new sweet potato ice cream from Mujirushi Ryohin, a.k.a. Muji, the lifestyle chain whose ice cream tends to be simple and understated, much like its furniture and housewares.

So, without further ado, let’s get started.

While Häagen-Dazs Japan brings out seasonal fall flavors on an annual basis, sweet potato isn’t always one of them. So we’d been getting a little anxious, but on September 15 they released their new Nou Mitsu Imo, or “Rich Sweet Potato,” flavor.

Pop the lid off, and you’re instantly greeted by a luxuriously lustrous glistening gold sweet potato sauce meant to evoke the sweet caramelized juices that ooze out of a freshly roasted sweet potato. The sauce is made with two of Japan’s most delicious sweet potato varieties, Beni Haruka (the sweetest variety in Japan) and anno imo.

Meanwhile, Mujirushi’s sweet potato ice cream flavor is just called Beni Haruka, and its English name, Sweet Potato Frozen Dessert, is starker still.

That name probably doesn’t have you expecting dazzling visuals, and sure enough, things are pretty plain under the lid.

▼ Hmm…those black dots do look intriguing, though…

In terms of visuals, there’s no denying that Häagen-Dazs is more attention-grabbing, and that’s where our spoon went first. True to its name, the Nou Mitsu Imo is rich and delicious. The sauce is thick but smooth, harmonizing excellently with the flavor and texture of the Beni Haruka ice cream, which has a bright yellow color to it.

With desserts that use this much sauce, you might be tempted to think they’re trying to cover up something or beat your taste buds into submission, but that’s not the case here. For all of its visual extravagance, Häagen-Dazs’ Nou Mitsu Imo is actually pretty straightforward. There are no ill-advised hidden ingredients or too-clever-for-its-own-good tricks involved, just lots and lots of great sweet potato flavor.

So after all that, would Mujirushi’s sweet potato ice cream come up short? Not at all! Remember those black dots we mentioned? It turns out they’re black sesame, and they’re not the only surprise that was waiting for us. As we dug down below the surface, we started coming across bits of actual sweet potato mixed in among the cream.

In addition to flavor, the sweet potato pieces added a lot of interesting texture, a crisp iciness with a fluffy chewiness waiting at the center. The black sesame imparted an elegantly enticing aroma, neither overpowering nor getting lost in the buttery notes of the sweet potato ice cream. All in all, it really delivers on the promise of “making the most of the ingredients’ flavors,” Mujirushi’s stated philosophy for its ice cream line.

Price-wise, there’s not much difference between the two, with Häagen-Dazs Nou Mitsu Imo at 373 yen (US$2.35) being just a touch more expensive than the 350-yen Mujirushi Beni Haruka. Muji’s ice cream is about 30 percent bigger (120 milliliters [4.1 ounce] vs. 90 milliliters), so it is technically the better value, but we think we can find room for both of these in our budget and stomach this fall.

title: Japanese convenience store is very focused with its new bento…maybe TOO focused
description: Lawson’s crazy corn bento arrives as part of new series of “sugi” foods. In Japanese, the suffix -sugi translates literally as “too” or “too much,” but it can also be used in the sense of “very.” This can sometimes make the intended meaning hard to understand. For example, if someone says their coworker isn’t just […]
content:
Lawson’s crazy corn bento arrives as part of new series of “sugi” foods.

In Japanese, the suffix -sugi translates literally as “too” or “too much,” but it can also be used in the sense of “very.” This can sometimes make the intended meaning hard to understand. For example, if someone says their coworker isn’t just yasahii (“kind”), but yasashisugi, that could either mean that they’re incredibly considerate, or it could mean that they’re overly, even problematically accommodating.

So generally you have to look at the overall context in which -sugi is being used, but even then, it’s not always easy to tell. For example, Japanese convenience store Lawson is getting set to release its new Ittentoppasugi line of bento boxed lunches. Ittentoppa basically means “single-minded,” which leaves us with the question of whether they’re extremely single-minded or too single-minded, and really, you could make an argument either way.

“JUST CORN” (コーンだけ), Lawson trumpets proudly in the promotional image for the new Ittentoppasugi Shikitsume Gohan Yaki Tomorokoshi, which, despite its lengthy name, really is just a whole lot of roasted corn (yaki tomorokoshi) served over a tray of rice (shikitsume Gohan). Those are the only ingredients, aside from the buttery soy sauce spread over the kernels.

But maybe you look at that box of corn and rice and can’t help thinking you’d like something with a little more protein? No problem, because Lawson’s focused/obsessive offerings continue with the Ittentoppasugi Shikitsume Gohan Teriyaki Sausage.

▼ As unartful as the presentation might be, teriyaki sauce and sausage actually are kind of a novel combination.

And finally, rounding out the Ittentoppasugi series is the Ittentoppasugi Shikitsume Gohan Bodakko, featuring a type of salted salmon popular in Akita Prefectue.

This one doesn’t match the quantity of its corn and sausage brethren, but it’s no less single-minded, perhaps to a depressingly spartan-looking degree. Speaking of which, Lawson describes all three of these as “bento,” which more commonly brings to mind boxed lunches with rice and a variety of side dishes (though bento does also sometimes get used for single-topping boxes/trays of rice too).

Now, if you’re someone who can’t get enough corn or sausage, or who appreciates salmon so much that you don’t want anything else getting in the way on your palate, then these Ittentoppasugi bento aren’t necessarily too ittentoppasugi, and for those who’re OK with this degree of single-mindedness, they are pretty reasonably priced. The corn and salmon bento are just 297 yen (US$1.85), and the sausage bento is 397 yen, far cheaper than just about any other convenience store bento these days.

On the other hand, some people are already voicing their opinion that Lawson has gone overboard with how laser-focused these concepts are, as shown in online comments such as:

“This is terrible. It’s like they just spread out a rice ball.”
“This is simple-sugi…and I’m intrigued.”
“You can just go ahead and write ‘Luxuries are forbidden’ on the packaging.”
“Thank you, Lawson, for taking pity on us poor people. I’ll be buying these.”
“That’s not single-minded, it’s shocking…I can’t get onboard with this.”
“Shouldn’t they leave this kind of stuff to the Lawson 100-yen [discount sister chain]?”

Lawson is actually also launching a line of luxurious zeitaku Zeitakusugi items at the same time, such as extra-meaty hiyashi chuka cold noodles with roast, stewed, and grilled pork (797 yen) and a whole box of Mont Blanc made with candied Japanese chestnuts (786 yen), though they don’t quite match the -sugi levels of the single-minded bento.

The Ittentoppasugi sausage and salmon both go on sale September 22, and the corn bento joins them one week later, on the 29th. Lawsone says they’ll all be on available “while supplies last,” though it doesn’t specify whether that’s referring to store stocks or the world supply of corn and sausage.

content:
Cosy up in colder weather with cute characters cuddling your toes.

With the days now getting colder in Japan, it’s time to start looking for cosy socks, and for Ghibli fans there’s no better way to stay warm than with some of the studio’s characters adorning your toes.

This year, Ghibli specialty shop chain Donguri Kyowakoku is giving fans a giant hug in the form of two new sock ranges, with the first being a collection of embroidered socks, honouring four of the studio’s popular movies.

These socks come with a cute little embroidered patch on the side, with cable-knit details giving each pair an elegant and stylish look.

▼ My Neighbour Totoro

The embroidering on the My Neighbour Totoro socks feature a circle of leaves to evoke the film’s forest setting, and in the middle is the Small Totoro, alongside a couple of acorns.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service

These socks feature Jiji, recalling the moment when the charismatic black cat steps in to act like a wide-eyed plush toy in a basket to help Kiki out when a mishap occurs during one of her deliveries.

▼ Spirited Away

This charming pair depicts Yu-bird, in tiny fly-like form, with a tea setting that recalls the visit to Zeniba’s house.

▼ Howl’s Moving Castle

title: Gang of angry monkeys surrounds and attacks Japanese man in hot spring town
description: Morning walk interrupted by notorious Troop T1. The town of Yugawara, in Kanagawa Prefecture, seems like it should be a very tranquil place. A seaside hot spring town, with baths and inns dotting the cityscape as it stretches up into the mountains as you head inland, it’s the sort of setting that entices you to […]
content:
Morning walk interrupted by notorious Troop T1.

The town of Yugawara, in Kanagawa Prefecture, seems like it should be a very tranquil place. A seaside hot spring town, with baths and inns dotting the cityscape as it stretches up into the mountains as you head inland, it’s the sort of setting that entices you to get up early and go for a nice stroll, and that’s how last Thursday started off for one local resident in his 40s.

Unfortunately, at about 6:50 in the morning, as he was walking past the entrance to one of the town’s inns, the man was suddenly surrounded by a group of roughly a dozen antagonists. When you find yourself outnumbered to that degree, ordinarily the smart thing to do is to try to talk your way out of the situation. That wasn’t an option, though, because the man wasn’t surrounded by yakuza thugs or delinquent youths, but by angry monkeys.

The animals advanced on the man, biting him several times on his hands before he could either get away or scare them off, and after reporting the incident he was taken to the hospital for treatment for his injuries.

▼ Monkeys on the streets of Yugawara

The trouble that had found the man this day came in the form of violent members of the group known as Troop T1, and if you’re thinking that a group of monkeys needs to acquire a certain degree of infamy, or at least notoriety, before a town gives them a name, you’re right. Monkeys in Yugawara have been growing increasingly bold. As you can see in the above video, they’re not limiting themselves to forested areas, with many of the animals now feeling comfortable roaming around more developed parts of the town. In 2025, there were over 900 reported incidents of monkeys behaving in an aggressive or intimidating manner towards human residents of Yugawara, including a farmer who said he was accosted by a group of monkeys in his field while harvesting melons and citrus fruits.

▼ Video from last winter, demonstrating how little apprehension some of the monkeys feel around people. In addition to raiding gardens, the animals have broken into homes by tearing through screen doors or prying open sliding glass ones.

As a hot spring town, tourism is a vital part of Yugawara’s economy, and as a rural town, many of its residents are elderly. Troop T1 preying on unsuspecting tourists or defenseless senior citizens. Since at least last year, the city administration has been seeking authorization from the Kanagawa prefectural government to capture all of Troop T1, but permission to do so has yet to be finalized.

It’s not clear what’s causing the increased aggression from the animals. Decades ago, it wasn’t uncommon for tourists to bring food into the Yugawara foothills to feed the monkeys with, which could erode the animals’ fear of humans and see them, and their living spaces, as sources of sustenance, but this has become far less prevalent than it used to be. All the same, the local authorities have reminded everyone to neither feed nor provoke the monkeys, and to contact the police should they spot groups of the animals in town.

On the bright side, at least Yugawara hasn’t had any bear troubles.

title: Fox spotted in Tokyo’s 23 wards, Japanese Internet wonders if it’s a shapeshifting spirit [Video]
description: Foxes rarely venture this close to the Tokyo city center…unless kitsune spirits are here all the time. You can spot lots of representations of foxes in Tokyo. Fox spirit sculptures often guard the entrance to shrines, and with the Japanese word for fox, “kitsune,” also being a way to describe soba or udon noodles served […]
content:
Foxes rarely venture this close to the Tokyo city center…unless kitsune spirits are here all the time.

You can spot lots of representations of foxes in Tokyo. Fox spirit sculptures often guard the entrance to shrines, and with the Japanese word for fox, “kitsune,” also being a way to describe soba or udon noodles served with fried tofu as a topping, it’s not unusual to come across illustrated foxes on restaurant signs, menus, or instant noodle packaging.

▼ You might even spot a fox tail accessory on someone keeping classic gyaru fashion alive.

But a real-life fox, walking around on the streets of one of Tokyo’s 23 central wards? The deforestation of the downtown and downtown-adjacent area over the past few generations means that’s something you won’t see very often at all, but that’s exactly what appears in this video recorded in Tokyo’s Nerima Ward on the night of September 13.

Nerima is more or less the northwest of the congregation of Tokyo’s 23 wards, but while it’s not as developed as, say, Shinjuku, Shibuya, or Toshima Wards, it’s not a rural outpost either, especially in the neighborhood shown in the video. Much of Nerima consists of residential housing for people who commute deeper into downtown for school or work, and deforestation means it’s been many years since foxes were a common sight in the area.

▼ Nerima Ward

Now, the scientific explanation for the fox seen in the video is that it’s what zoologists call an “urban fox,” meaning a fox that’s adapted to finding food and shelter in ab area primarily habituated by humans. However, several online commenters have floated alternate theories drawing on Japanese folklore. According to legend, Japanese fox spirits have the ability to transform, and they sometimes take on the guise of humans and walk among us without anyone noticing, until they have a lapse in concentration and reveal their true form. With those stories in mind, comments on the video have included:

“Gotta be a young fox who’s still getting the hang of his transformation powers.”
“I bet he spends his afternoon as a hardworking salaryman.”
“Maybe he had a busy day and now he’s tired and forgot to keep up his transformation.”
“Probably changing back from his human form at the end of the day so that he can go do fox stuff.”
“I bet if you chased after him, you’d end up at a shrine.”
“Much happier to hear about this than another bear sighting.”
“’Urban Fox’ sounds cool! They should make a clothing brand called that.”
“Just like tanuki, there are kitsune who pretend to be humans living in the city.”
“It’s like something out of the Pompoko Ghibli anime.”

▼ For reference, the Ghibli movie Pompoko, about a group of shapeshifting tanuki losing their habitat due to the construction of a human housing development in the early 1990s, is set in the Tama New Town area, which is farther from the Tokyo city center than where the Nerima fox was seen.

▼ Tama New Town

The comments are most likely meant more as tongue-in-cheek jokes than actual belief in transforming spirits, but in all seriousness, as cute as foxes may be, it’s important to remember that foxes can be carriers of parasitic tapeworms which can be transmitted to humans and lead to the growth of harmful tumors on internal organs, and incubation periods of up to 15 years can complicate diagnosing a patient’s condition once they do start to show symptoms. In other words, contacting with a wild fox could be just as harmful as running afoul of the sinister fox spirits in the darker legends about them so if you do happen to come across a Tokyo kitsune, make sure to keep a respectful distance.

title: JAL first class cakes can be bought for a bargain, but are they as bougie as they seem?
description: In Japan, a cake that’s “imperfect” can sometimes be perfect. Whenever we’re not eating sweets, you can find us on the Internet, searching for sweets, and the rarer they are, the better. So when our reporter Natsuki Gojo discovered an odd-looking pack of cakes online, she immediately stopped browsing, and when she leaned in and […]
content:
In Japan, a cake that’s “imperfect” can sometimes be perfect.

Whenever we’re not eating sweets, you can find us on the Internet, searching for sweets, and the rarer they are, the better. So when our reporter Natsuki Gojo discovered an odd-looking pack of cakes online, she immediately stopped browsing, and when she leaned in and discovered that it was a kilo (2.2 pounds) of cake ends from the cakes served to Japan Airlines’ first-class passengers, she wasted no time in clicking the purchase button.

Marked as “wake ari” (“imperfect”), Urokoya Sohonten’s “Premium Cake Ends” are inherently imperfect – as off-cuts from the manufacturing process, they would usually be discarded rather than presented for serving. The taste is the same as the more beautiful bits in between the ends, though, and given that they’re made by a long-established confectionery shop founded in 1684, Natsuki was far more interested in the flavour than the presentation.

Still, when they arrived on her doorstep, the cake ends looked beautiful to her eye, with two packs containing four neat towers, and each pack weighing around 500 grams.

Though she’d thought that “cake ends” might turn out to be small bits and leftover scraps, these were far bigger than she imagined, and looked like cakes in their own right.

▼ Comparing the size with a Sylvanian Families baby, and a human hand, gives you an idea of just how big these cakes are.


▼ Plenty of thickness in both the sponge and fresh cream.

She was surprised by how hefty they were too, because when she went to take a selfie with them, she found they were difficult to hold.

The cake ends arrive frozen, which is great as you can thaw only as much as you want to eat.

▼ The pack comes with stickers for jotting down the date you thaw it.

Each slice is about 16–17 centimetres (6.3–6.7 inches) long and a little over 1.5 centimetres (0.6 inches) thick, so it’s a generous serving.

After opening the pack and popping one of the slices on a plate, Natsuki cut it in half, which made it basically the same size as a regular piece of cake. Taking a taste, it was just as delicious as she’d hoped, with a dense yet fluffy sponge adding a soft sweetness to the fresh cream sandwiched inside of it.

The fresh cream was only mildly sweet, so Natsuki felt like she could easily eat to her heart’s content, and the flavours were incredibly well-balanced, which is a sign of a well-made, high-quality sweet.

▼ So this is what First Class tastes like!

While the cake can be eaten as is, because the flavour is simple, you can customise it to your liking. Natsuki chopped up the other half and added chocolate sauce, nuts and mint to make a decadent mini parfait, and it was utterly delicious.

With every mouthful, Natsuki felt like she was enjoying both a stylish cafe experience and a taste of first-class luxury in her own home. She now says she might just be hooked on these first-class cakes, and is chuffed that she found them.

If you’d like to enjoy a taste of first-class while not up in the air, these cakes can be purchased at the online store, as well as online retail sites like Amazon and Rakuten. According to the official website, a kilo of these cakes is equivalent to about 11 slices of shortcake, so at 3,999 yen (US$25.84), including postage, this is a very sweet deal.

title: Naked illuminates Kyoto’s cultural traditions in Nijo Castle’s latest digital art spectacular
description: Featuring night-lit gardens, imperial poetry, and custom digital garments. Kyoto is home to an abundance of heritage fused with modernity: a place where you could espy a traditional building from afar only to discover a familiar mermaid emblazoned on the sign when you draw closer. Tokyo-based creative collective Naked, Inc., known for combining cinematic storytelling […]
content:
Featuring night-lit gardens, imperial poetry, and custom digital garments.

Kyoto is home to an abundance of heritage fused with modernity: a place where you could espy a traditional building from afar only to discover a familiar mermaid emblazoned on the sign when you draw closer. Tokyo-based creative collective Naked, Inc., known for combining cinematic storytelling with cutting-edge technology, embraces this dichotomy wholeheartedly, having run several digital art exhibitions over the years in some of Japan’s most iconic landmarks, including Himeji Castle and Matsushima. Running from October 23 through December 5, the immersive art exhibition Naked Meets Nijo Castle 2026 once again transforms the castle grounds into a glowing canvas of light, sound, and interactive digital art.

Originally built in 1603 as the Kyoto residence of the Tokugawa shogun, Nijo Castle is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site famed for its stunning traditional architecture and spacious gardens. The 2026 exhibition celebrates the 400th anniversary of the 1626 Kanei Gyoko (Imperial Visit), a momentous five-day event when Emperor Go-Mizunoo visited the castle, sparking a cultural exchange between the imperial court and the samurai elite, with cultural aspects like tea ceremony and flower arrangement blossoming. The shogunate used the event as a chance to legitimize their de facto rule over the now-unified country, whereas the emperor took the opportunity to show the country that the imperial family was still relevant in the current period.

To bring this historic era to life, Naked, Inc. draws inspiration from Tokugawa Masako, the daughter of the shogun and empress consort to Emperor Go-Mizunoo. A central figure of the Kanei era (1624-1645), Masako bridged courtly elegance and samurai culture, leaving a lasting influence on Japanese aesthetic traditions, including the delicate art of the kimono.

As a collaboration with the larger Kanei Gyoko 400th Anniversary Festival, with events being held both within Kyoto and nationwide, visitors to Naked meets Nijo Castle 2026 will encounter a total of three curated zones to enjoy. The journey begins at the grand Karamon Gate (a grand Chinese-style gate featuring intricate wood carvings), illuminated with vivid digital projections displaying class Kanei-era patterns and colors.

As you wander past the Ninomaru Palace, inner moat, and Seiryuen Garden, light and sound installations weave together waka poetry composed by Masako, traditional gosho-zome (imperial court dyeing techniques), and illuminated garden scenery.

In the kitchen forecourt, guests can participate in interactive art, selecting classic design patterns to project directly onto a white kosode (a traditional short-sleeved garment that served as the predecessor to the modern kimono) to wear as digital fashion. Guests can also enjoy Masako’s Night Tea Party, combining art, atmosphere, and traditional tea culture.

The exhibition takes place daily from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., with admission nightly until 9:00 p.m. Advance tickets are available at major Japanese convenience stores and travel companies Jalan and Rakuten Travel (all links below), until October 22 starting at 1,600 yen for weekdays and 2,000 yen for weekends, but standard tickets are 2,000 yen for Mondays to Thursdays and 2,400 yen for weekends and holidays. If you are fortunate to be a student or Kyoto resident, a cashback of 500 yen is offered at the on-site booth with a valid ID.

For anyone eager to experience Kyoto’s cultural heritage through a modern lens, this event promises an unforgettable autumn evening, but for those looking to get more hands on, Naked also recently opened a traditional craft workshop at Kyoto Station.

title: New Gundam Base superstores coming soon in the U.S., with one opening this month
description: Bandai Namco’s store that’s all about anime Mobile Suits is moving into new territories. content:
Bandai Namco’s store that’s all about anime Mobile Suits is moving into new territories.

There’s a Gundam-shaped, and also Gundam-sized, hole in the hearts of anime enthusiasts in Tokyo these days, as August 31 was the last day for the city’s life-size Gundam statue before the start of its dismantling process. But as Gundam fans in Tokyo dry their tears, it’s time for their counterparts in America to start smiling, because the U.S. is getting two new Gundam Base superstores this summer, and the opening of the first is happening in less than two weeks.

The Gundam Base Minneapolis will be opening inside the Mall of America on September 30, becoming America’s second Gundam Base, following the opening of Gundam Base Chicago in 2025. The harshness of winters in the American Midwest representing high potential demand for indoor activities such as anime and plastic model kits notwithstanding, it might seem a little unusual for the region to be getting both of America’s initial Gundam Bases, but the Mall of America is the biggest shopping center in the country, so it should provide ample space for a vast array of Gunpla model kits, figures, and other merch, as well as space for special in-store events and celebrations.

Opening on the same day, and right next door to the Gundam Base Minneapolis, will be a new Bandai Namco Cross Store, carrying a wide variety of otaku-oriented items from the many, many franchises the company does merchandising for, ranging from Gashapon capsule toys and high-end Tamashii Nations figures to lifestyle goods and stationery.

Bandai Namco is trumpeting that Gundam Base Minneapolis will have “exclusive merchandise,” though right now that seems to mean they’re exclusive to Gundam Base stores, not the Minneapolis branch specifically. Either way, the MG 1/100 The Gundam Base Limited RX-78-2 Ver. 3.0 [The Gundam Base Color] and RG 1/144 The Gundam Base Limited Wing Gundam Zero EW [Clear Color] do look very cool.

▼ Yes, we’ve now reached the point in the timeline where Gundam models have even longer names than the in-anime mecha.

Later this fall the Gundam Base will also be expanding outside the American Midwest to simply the American West, as Seattle is getting a Gundam Base of its own at Westfield Southcenter, though an exact opening date doesn’t appear to have been publicly announced yet.

It’s worth noting that no announcement has been made what’s going to become of the dismantled components of Tokyo’s Unicorn Gundam statue, and the whereabouts of the 1:1-scale original Gundam statue are also undisclosed following its stints in Yokohama and Osaka . Even if a full on-site rebuild wouldn’t be feasible in terms of space, the opening of new Gundam Bases in the U.S. would seem like a prime opportunity to at least display the statues’ heads, but Bandai Namco has only said that “grand opening celebrations, exclusive merchandise, and special events for each location will be announced closer to their respective opening dates.”

title: Tokyo’s Square Burger claims it’s a viral hit with foreign tourists who’ve given it near-perfect Google reviews
description: Burger stand near Tokyo’s most famous temple has local partners with more than 100 years of history helping the Square Burger stick out from the crowd. They say nobody’s perfect, but with an average out to 4.9 out of 5 stars as of this month for Kadomasu-The Square Burger, the Tokyo restaurant’s Google user reviews […]
content:
Burger stand near Tokyo’s most famous temple has local partners with more than 100 years of history helping the Square Burger stick out from the crowd.

They say nobody’s perfect, but with an average out to 4.9 out of 5 stars as of this month for Kadomasu-The Square Burger, the Tokyo restaurant’s Google user reviews say the place is about as close to perfection as you can get. This isn’t a case of the restaurant lucking out with a string of its earliest customers all coincidentally happening to like the place before a larger sample pool pulls ratings down, either, as those 4.9 stars are the average from across more than 2,000 customer reviews.

As you can probably guess from its name, the star of the menu at Kadomasu-The Square Burger is the Square Burger. To illustrate just how proud they are of the sandwich, the restaurant used to just be called Kadomasu, but since the Square Burger was added to the menu last spring, the management says that it’s been generating a huge amount of positive buzz on social media among foreign tourists traveling in Tokyo. Kadomasu-The Square Burger also says that over 80 percent of their customers are visitors from overseas.

Kadomasu (which also serves steak skewers, desserts, and drinks) is located in Tokyo’s Asakusa neighborhood, not far from the famous Sensoji Temple. For its patties, it uses A5-grade wagyu beef, but why are its burgers square? There’s at least a little wordplay involved — the “kado” part of Kadomasu is the Japanese word for “corner.” Being square, though, also lets the patties match the shape of the bread that’s used for the burgers.

Yes, that’s right, bread, not buns. As an Asakusa restaurant, Kadomasu wants to make a uniquely Asakusa burger, and they say they get their bread from local bakery Terasawa, which was founded in the neighborhood in 1950. The Square Burger’s bread is specially made for the sandwich, with golden sesame seeds kneaded into it for a nutty accent, and toasted on the restaurant’s flat grill with a generous amount of butter, cooked to achieve a crispness on its outer surface but a soft fluffiness closer to its center. Said bread is delivered to the restaurant, freshly baked, every morning, personally by Terasawa’s third-generation owner, Masahiko Terasawa, according to the management.

The partner for Kadomasu’s burger sauce has an even longer history. Sauce maker Tokiha Sauce has been part of the Asakusa neighborhood since 1923, and after a few extra ingredients are added to Tokiha’s vegetable-based Nama Sauce, it becomes the spread for Kadomasu’s Square Burger.

The Square Burger is served sliced for easier eating, cut into square quarters, naturally. A dollop of wasabi comes on the side for those that want to add some spiciness, and if you want even more decadent richness than the wagyu beef and buttered bread are going to provide, you can order it with cheddar cheese too.

Though Kadomasu-The Square Burger makes its stance very clear as to whether or not a sandwich has to have a bun in order to be called a burger, there are a few mysteries about the place. For starters, while its 4.9-star Google review average holds up as of this writing (currently from 2,028 reviews), aside from the press release images seen in this article, the only customer-uploaded photo of the signature sandwich floating around online seems to be the one on Japanese restaurant info site Tabelog here. Kadomasu-The Square Burger is also less than forthcoming about how much the Square Burger costs. The restaurant has no website (and thus no online menu), and its official Instagram account doesn’t list prices for its items. That’s not to say on-site customers don’t know how much they’re going to be charged for their sandwich, though, since there’s a signboard posted outside its entrance with prices listed. Photos taken at the restaurant in August show that the price at the time was 2,850 yen (US$18) for the Square Burger and 3,150 yen if you wanted it with cheese, though being in a tourist-oriented part of town, it’s possible that the price could have changed since then.

title: Hatsune Miku/Hokusai exhibition in Tokyo lets you make your own Miku woodblock print
description: Printing Museum hosts mini exhibition for crossover of virtual idol and ukiyo-e art. As Japan’s first virtual idol, Hatsune Miku was a major milestone in the digital art field. She wasn’t the countries first example of making art by non-traditional methods, though, as centuries before painter Katsushika Hokusai’s ukiyo-e creations were produced using woodblock printing, […]
content:
Printing Museum hosts mini exhibition for crossover of virtual idol and ukiyo-e art.

As Japan’s first virtual idol, Hatsune Miku was a major milestone in the digital art field. She wasn’t the countries first example of making art by non-traditional methods, though, as centuries before painter Katsushika Hokusai’s ukiyo-e creations were produced using woodblock printing, helping to greatly expand the scope of art appreciation among the common people.

Back in the summer, we even looked at a collaboration of sorts between the two icons, in which Miku and her fellow Vocaloids visit Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views of Mt. Fuji with a little help from illustrator Rella.

Initially, the crossover artwork was only being offered for sale as part of a merchandise line, but now they’re getting the proper museum treatment, with a mini exhibition at Tokyo’s Printing Museum.

「葛飾北斎×初音ミク」コラボのデザインのミクのねんどろいどは、
印刷博物館ミニ展示「Polaris －時代を超えた アイコンと絵師－」にて展示します。
皆様のご来場をお待ちしています。

会期：2026年9月19日(土)〜2027年1月11日(月・祝)
会場：印刷博物館B1プロローグ#北斎ミク展 #初音ミク… https://t.co/y16ZgHTgWH pic.twitter.com/kIc9y9Tcmd

— 印刷博物館 PrintingMuseum (@PrintingMuseumT) September 15, 2026

In addition to the crossover artwork, the museum will also be displaying reproductions of the original Hokusai pieces that serve as the backgrounds, with explanations of the step-by-step process of how ukiyo-e are made by adding one layer of color at a time through differently shaped woodblock stamps, until final the complete picture is formed.

The exhibition also includes clever ideas such as inserting a figure of the Great Wave off Kanagawa-version of Miku into a diorama of the Hokusai painting that inspired her outfit and Rela’s ukiyo-e Vocaloid designs printed not onto paper, but skateboard decks.

 

But arguably the coolest part of the event is an ukiyo-e stamping workshop where you can make your own copy of the super-deformed version of the Great Wave Miku painting.

Admission to the museum, which has a number of other, non-Vocaloid-related displays as well, is just 550 yen (US$3.50), with an additional charge of 500 yen more for the ukiyo-e workshop. Odds are that’ll still leave you with plenty of room in your budget, and the museum’s giftshop will also be offering prints, pins, keyholders, fans, and other Vocaloid ukiyo-e items.

Polaris -Icons and Artists Across the Ages-, as the mini exhibition is officially titled runs from September 19 to January 11.

title: Bear spotted near most popular hiking trail on Tokyo’s most popular hiking mountain
description: Officials calling for caution as Mt. Takao enters peak hiking season. Fall is, by far, the best time of year to go hiking in Japan. content:
Officials calling for caution as Mt. Takao enters peak hiking season.

Fall is, by far, the best time of year to go hiking in Japan. Free from worries about the snows of winter, the hay fever-triggering pollen of spring, or the debilitating heat and humidity of summer, a stroll along a mountain trail is one of the best ways to spend a crisp, clear autumn day. You don’t even have to venture all that far from the big city to find good hiking. Mt. Takao is only an hour train ride west of the Tokyo city center, and the 599-meter (1,965-foot) tall mountain makes for a fun and accessible trek, taking about two hours to hike to the summit and another 90 minutes or so to get back down.

However, officials are calling for visitors to Tokyo’s favorite day-hike destination to be cautious, following a bear sighting near its most popular trail.

Out of the multiple routes to the top of Takao, Trail 1 is the most popular. Also called the Omotesando Route, it takes you through a nice mixture of natural scenery and man-made landmarks, such as the atmospheric Yakuoin Temple. On Wednesday, though, Hachioji City, the district of Tokyo in which Mt. Takao is located, announced that video from observation cameras installed on the mountain had shown an adult Asian black bear near the trail.

▼ Mt. Takao’s Trail 1

The bear’s presence didn’t come to light until sometime after the fact, with volunteers noticing it on video recorded at around 11 p.m. on August 20. The sighting was reported to the central Tokyo Metropolitan Government, who confirmed that the animal seen in the images was indeed a black bear and then informed Hachioji City.

It should be noted that the animal was roughly 70 meters (230 feet) from the path, and bears have been known to inhabit the area. Still, this is evidently closer than bears usually get to Trail 1.

▼ The bear was reported as being seen in the vicinity of where Trail 1 crosses over the expressway’s Takasosan Tunnel, which wouldn’t be far from the section seen here, which is about a 30 to 40-minute walk from the start of the trail.

With the bear having come closer to the trail than normal, and also bear attacks in general becoming more frequent in recent years, Hachioji officials are understandably concerned, especially as upcoming autumn holidays and the changing colors of the fall leaves will be drawing many people to the mountain in the weeks to come. They’re advising that visitors avoid hiking in early morning, evening, and nighttime hours, to hike with a friend or as part of a group, and to attach either a bell or a radio to their bag or belt, all to prevent startling any bears and triggering an aggressive response.

title: Starbucks Japan unveils Mitsuimo Milk, a new drink that celebrates the taste of autumn
description: Limited-edition beverage introduces us to the magic that happens when you roast a Japanese sweet potato. In Japan, the arrival of autumn brings with it a bounty of seasonal produce, and one of the harvest stars is sweet potato. It’s a vegetable so popular it’s become one of the season’s signature flavours, and Starbucks is […]
content:
Limited-edition beverage introduces us to the magic that happens when you roast a Japanese sweet potato.

In Japan, the arrival of autumn brings with it a bounty of seasonal produce, and one of the harvest stars is sweet potato. It’s a vegetable so popular it’s become one of the season’s signature flavours, and Starbucks is celebrating its sweetness in a simple yet stunning new special release.

Called Mitsuimo Milk, this beverage is made with beni haruka, one of the most popular varieties of sweet potato in Japan, beloved for its well-rounded sweetness. Mitsuimo (literally “honey potato”), is the term used to describe sweet potatoes that are so sweet the natural sugars become densely concentrated, oozing out a honey-like syrup when baked – a quality that beni haruka is renowned for.

For locals, the word “mitsuimo” is enough to make them salivate, and Starbucks has already witnessed its powers of seduction firsthand, through the popularity of the Melty Mitsuimo Frappuccino and Melty Mitsuimo Mousse Tea Latte released earlier this month.

Whereas those two drinks (pictured above) were filled with richness and multiple layers of flavour, this new release strips away the trimmings, offering a simpler, more pared-back take on the sweet potato to showcase the depths of its honey-like sweetness.

By blending baked sweet potato paste with smooth milk, customers will be able to enjoy a deliciously creamy texture that mimics the mouthfeel of a sweet potato. The simplicity of the ingredients helps to showcase the delicate, nuanced flavours that are naturally inherent in the vegetable and unlocked through the baking process, when it sings with syrupy sweetness.

If you’ve ever wondered what it’s like to drink a sweet potato unfettered by other seasonal ingredients, then the Mitsuimo Milk will open the door to a new realm of deliciousness. Priced at 618 yen (US$4.10) for takeout or 630 yen for dine-in, the new drink will be available at Starbucks stores around Japan from 18 September.

title: Free Mt. Fuji helicopter rescues for offseason hikers are ending in Yamanashi
description: Governor asks offseason hikers to “stop waving around their freedom to climb the mountain as if it’s the only thing that matters.” As the country’s most famous landmark, Mt. Fuji inspires musings on Japan’s history, culture, and natural beauty. Unfortunately, in recent years it also evokes thoughts of irresponsible, overconfident offseason hikers who ignore safety […]
content:
Governor asks offseason hikers to “stop waving around their freedom to climb the mountain as if it’s the only thing that matters.”

As the country’s most famous landmark, Mt. Fuji inspires musings on Japan’s history, culture, and natural beauty. Unfortunately, in recent years it also evokes thoughts of irresponsible, overconfident offseason hikers who ignore safety warnings and need someone to come and save them, and growing public frustration has lead to a new rule under which some of them will have to pay the bill for their own rescue.

To recap, the official climbing season on Mt. Fuji runs from early July to early September. Outside of that period, Mt. Fuji is said to be “closed,” but its off-season status is somewhat complicated. Technically, it’s the trails that lead from Mt. Fuji’s fifth station (where paved streets stop) up to the top of the mountain that are off-limits. The trails are classified as prefectural roads, and so Yamanashi and Shizuoka, the two prefectures Mt. Fuji straddles, have the authority to bar their use during the fall, winter, and spring.

However, ascending past the fifth station during the offseason, in and of itself, is not illegal, and in recent years an increasing number of people have been trying to summit Fuji outside the climbing season. An increasing number of them have also been failing to do so, requiring rescue teams to be dispatched to come and pick them up and carry them home. During the offseason, when there’s less daylight, more snow, and fewer support personnel on/near the mountain, rescue operations become more difficult, as well as more dangerous for the workers involved.

And so, in a press conference on September 14, four days after Yamanashi Prefecture’s Yoshida Mt. Fuji trail closed for the year, Governor Kotaro Nagasaki announced that the prefecture will be installing a new ordinance in which offseason climbers requiring evacuation by helicopter from Mt. Fuji will be charged for the operation.

▼ “Will you be paying by cash, credit, or Suica card, sir?”

The amount rescued hikers will have to pay will be based on expenses such as fuel and personnel costs. As such, the bill will likely vary depending on the complexity of the operation and the distance of the flight to necessary medical facilities. For reference, in Saitama Prefecture, which already has ordinances charging negligent hikers for their rescues, a five-minute helicopter ride carries a charge of around 8,000 yen (US$50).

▼ Governor Nagasaki’s press conference

Addressing the ostensible sentiment of offseason hikers that, because it’s not illegal, they’re free to climb Mt. Fuji outside the official season, Nagasaki said:

“In the event that they do end up needing to be rescued, we are obligated to help them, which puts rescue workers in danger, so I would like them to stop waving around their freedom to climb the mountain as if it’s the only thing that matters.”

Nagasaki did add, though, that rescue fees could be reduced or waived for offseason hikers who file an offseason hiking notification and are judged to have properly prepared for their climb. However, with the prefecture’s official stance being that Mt. Fuji is too dangerous to climb during that part of the year, it seems unlikely that the authorities will be prone to judging offseason climbers’ preparations as adequate, especially when those hikes ended up unable to get home from Mt. Fuji under their own power.

Online reactions to the plan to charge offseason hikers for helicopter rescues have included:

“There’s no need to use taxpayer money to rescue people who don’t follow the rules.”
“The people who have to go rescue them end up having to put their lives in danger too.”
“They should have done this years ago.”
“No need to reduce the charges for anyone. Whether you’re ‘prepared’ or not, if you’re hiking in the offseason, you take responsibility.”
“How about if we just say ‘Offseason hiking is dangerous, so there will be no rescue operations. Please take responsibility for yourself.”
“Freedom comes with responsibilities.”
“Honestly they should just make it illegal to hike Mt. Fuji in the offseason.”

That last idea likely is something that Yamanashi and Shizuoka would like to do, but the current system of barring access to the prefectural-road trails suggests that making the mountain as a whole off-limits during the offseason is probably something that can’t be easily done from a legal-framework standpoint.

Yamanashi’s offseason helicopter rescue charges are expected to go into effect in the fall of 2027.

Like Yamanashi, Shizuoka Prefecture is also planning to introduce a new ordinance that would require hikers to file a notification before attempting to climb Mt. Fuji in the offseason. Neither prefecture has clarified what the process for filing the notification will be, but it’s unlikely to be quick and convenient, since the notification system’s main purpose seems to be to act as a de-facto deterrent to offseason hiking by making possible penalties for noncompliance even if the prefectures can’t yet make offseason hiking itself illegal.

title: “Lineup” begins for iPhone18 in Tokyo
description: It’s more of a pointup than a lineup though. On 16 September, our veteran reporter Mr. Sato was strolling through Tokyo’s Omotesando neighborhood. It was a rather wet and miserable day, as many this autumn seem to be, but at least things were cooling down from the intense summer. He looked around at all the […]
content:
It’s more of a pointup than a lineup though.

On 16 September, our veteran reporter Mr. Sato was strolling through Tokyo’s Omotesando neighborhood. It was a rather wet and miserable day, as many this autumn seem to be, but at least things were cooling down from the intense summer.

He looked around at all the shops, some new, some old, but one that has really stood the test of time was the SoftBank Omotesando shop. That place was special to Mr. Sato as it was the first place he ever lined up to be one of the first to purchase the iPhone 4 back in 2010. “Has it really been 16 years?” he thought to himself.

Our writer was thinking about how a person born that year would be in high school by now, when he suddenly spotted something peculiar in front of the SoftBank… It was an orange mohawk.

Orange mohawks are a rare sight in Japan, so Mr. Sato was fairly certain it was none other than Butch a.k.a. Big Wave.

Mr. Sato: “Butch! What are you doing standing out in the rain?!”

Butch: “Oh, s’up bruh!!!”

Mr. Sato: “Aren’t you cold? What are you doing out here?”

Butch: “Pffft, like you don’t know… It’s the event of the century, bruh! The iPhone! The new iPhone is coming out! And when a new iPhone launches, that’s my cue, baby!”

Mr. Sato: “Oh, is that this week? So, it’s already time for that crazy expensive phone to come out.”

Butch: “That’s right! Don’t tell me you forgot, bruh. What happened to the guy who used to line up with me back in the day?”

Mr. Sato: “Yeah, I totally forgot. I’m actually using an Android now, so I haven’t been keeping track of the release dates.”

Butch: “Dang, I guess changing to Android makes you a really dull guy too.”

Mr. Sato: “I just lost interest. I don’t think it’s the phone’s fault.”

Butch: “If you say so, bruh.”

Not wanting to stand out in the rain any longer, Mr. Sato wished Butch well and went on his way.

As he walked, Mr. Sato looked back on those days. For a brief moment in history, iPhone launches were major cultural events, and Mr. Sato was right in the middle of it all. For two years in a row, he first person in Japan to purchase a new iPhone model after its launch, rubbing shoulders with celebrities like Ken Watanabe at the celebratory ceremony.

▼  Mr. Sato was celebrated as the first iPhone5S owner in Japan in 2013.

And it was on the iPhone line circuit that he met Butch, whose eye-catching appearance and effervescent attitude made him a constant presence on TV news coverage of iPhone releases.

▼ News report of the iPhone3G release in 2008. Butch can be seen a little under a minute into it.

He even managed to parlay that into acting and modeling work, appearing as the mascot for Taco Bell Japan at one point.

However, as the years passed, the excitement of yet another iPhone that wasn’t hugely different from the year before dwindled. At the same time, Mr. Sato grew older. Now in his 50s, he doubted he had the stamina to spend three days and nights on a sidewalk.

Butch is younger by about 10 years, but is just getting to that age where aches and pains become more frequent, and the invincibility of youth begins to falter. And yet, he still tirelessly shows up every year to camp out on the sidewalk and wait for the new iPhone, even after the rest of the world has moved on.

▼Butch in 2024

Mr. Sato began to feel bad for his friend and decided that the next day he would hold an intervention for him on the sidewalk in front of the SoftBank Omotesando.

On 17 September, Mr. Sato returned to the lineup for the iPhone18, which consisted solely of Butch. As he approached, he thought that perhaps if he could show his pal how far Android has come along in terms of performance and affordability, perhaps he could finally pack up his lawn chair and pursue a new hobby.

Mr. Sato: “Butch, it’s been raining non-stop. Are you alright?!”

Butch: “Bruh, do I look alright to you? I’m cold and wet, and my lower back is killing me, dog.”

Mr. Sato: “Butch, it’s over. The iPhone dream is dead, man. It’s time to wake up and see that!”

Butch: “But, bruh… It’s just… I…”

Mr. Sato: “Enough. Android is pretty good too, you know. If you still think it’s that sluggish phone of a decade ago, you’re wrong, man. The world has changed. The iPhone isn’t the only game in town anymore.”

Butch: “But the release date is coming up…”

Mr. Sato: “You damn fool! Even the cheapest iPhone is 219,800 yen (US$1,400) and the 2TB iPhone 18 Pro is freaking 449,800 yen ($2,900)! Forgetting about specs, you can get a brand new Android for just 22,000 yen ($141)! Don’t you see?!”

Butch: “That’s not it, bruh. I mean… I…”

Mr. Sato: “Listen to me, Butch. You’ve done enough. You led the charge on iPhone releases, made “you gotta ride this Big Wave” a popular catchphrase, and inspired the nation with your ASCII art.”

“But look around you. There are fewer and fewer young people who even know what ASCII art is, let alone an iPhone lineup. The iPhone 3G came out 18 years ago, man. Isn’t it time to hang up your mohawk? Android is really pretty decent now.”

Butch: “Bruh, you totally got it twisted…”

Butch: “It’s just that I…”

Butch: “I LOVE THE LINE!”

Butch: “I don’t care about the iPhone… I care about lining up!”

Butch’s admission gave Mr. Sato pause. Indeed, Big Wave had eluded to being more a fan of lining up for iPhones than the iPhones themselves in past years. Our reporter realized he took the completely wrong approach in trying to make Butch see the light.

Mr. Sato: “Of course… You were never lining up to buy an iPhone. You always lined up just to be in the line.”

Defeated, Mr. Sato once again wished Butch well and went on his way back to his dry and heated home. He wondered how long Butch would continue to be a lineup of one in front of the SoftBank Omotesando now that the rest of the world has moved on.

Perhaps he could find his friend something more popular to line up for these days, something with other people so that Butch could find that joy and excitement of waiting again, and something that didn’t cost as much as a used car.

title: Starbucks Corporation is planning to sell off Starbucks Japan, report says
description: Do Starbuck Japan and Starbucks U.S.A. not need each other anymore? Like 7-Eleven and McDonald’s, Starbucks has become an originally American brand that many travelers will tell you does things a little differently, and better, in Japan. Known for quality and creativity, Starbucks Japan is constantly cycling new, seasonal items in and out of its […]
content:
Do Starbuck Japan and Starbucks U.S.A. not need each other anymore?

Like 7-Eleven and McDonald’s, Starbucks has become an originally American brand that many travelers will tell you does things a little differently, and better, in Japan. Known for quality and creativity, Starbucks Japan is constantly cycling new, seasonal items in and out of its menu, like its recent sweet potato and kyoho grape Frappuccinos, with pretty much each and every one getting a thumbs-up from satisfied customers.

And yet, it looks like Starbucks Corporation, the chain’s Seattle-based parent company, is getting ready to sell Starbucks Japan, according to Reuters, which cites unnamed sources “with knowledge of the matter.”

It doesn’t take more than a few minutes walking around any large city in Japan to see that Starbucks is incredibly popular here. There may not be a branch on literally every corner, but as of September of last year, there were 1,883 Starbucks Japan locations, accounting for 9 percent of all the Starbucks coffeehouses in the world. Starbucks’ first branch in Japan, which opened in Tokyo’s Ginza neighborhood in 1996, was also its first location outside of North America. With a market value of approximately US$3 billion/470 billion yen, Starbucks Japan is also the largest Starbucks market outside of the U.S. that’s directly controlled by Starbucks Corporation.

Starbucks Corporation became the sole stockholder of Starbucks Japan in 2014, when it purchased the 60.5 percent of the company’s stock that had been held by Sazaby League, the Japanese lifestyle company behind such ventures as the Afternoon Tea chain of cafes/housewares stores and apparel brand Agnes B. Starbucks Corporation paid US$914 million for its stake, and in the 12 years since Starbucks Japan’s market value has doubled, and it’s nearly doubled its number of branches from the 1,050 it then had.

▼ There’s even a Starbucks with a great view of Osaka’s famous mecha crab.

Starbucks Corporation’s reported interest in selling off a majority stake in Starbucks Japan doesn’t stem from underperformance by the Japanese coffeehouses, though. Instead, it appears to be part of a reassessment of Starbucks Corporation’s global assets with the goal of greater focus on the U.S., where the chain’s profits are slumping. Reuters reports that Starbucks Corporation was advised in June that “the [Japanese] market is not central to Starbucks’ brand,” and that selling off control of Starbucks Japan could give them monetary resources and free up upper Starbucks Corporation executives to circle the wagons in their home market.

The idea that the Japanese market isn’t all that important to Starbucks’ image as a brand might seem strange, given the chain’s massive popularity in the country. However, there’s only a limited amount of perceptive synergy between the chain’s Japanese and American branches. Many of the most popular and buzz-generating items at Starbucks Japan are originals created for the Japanese market, and not many of them make the trip across the Pacific to join the Starbucks U.S.A. menu (matcha Frappuccinos notwithstanding). Once again, similar to McDonald’s and 7-Eleven, Starbucks has now been operating in Japan for so long, and does so much to cater to local tastes, that its Japanese consumers aren’t really coming in because they’re craving an “American!” experience, so in and of itself, non-American ownership probably won’t be an issue. Likewise, when Starbucks customers in America look at their drink and food options, they’re not seeing a lot that come from Japan. Sure, at the time of Starbucks’ arrival in Japan, its pedigree as a famous American chain helped it attract attention and inspired consumer trust, but nowadays, neither Starbucks Japan not Starbucks U.S.A. owe much of their success, or lack thereof, to each other.

▼ The mottainai banana affogato Frappuccino, one of many Japan-exclusives

At the same time, Starbucks consistent popularity in Japan, at least from customers’ point of view, feels very much like “If it’s not broken, don’t try to fix it” sort of situation. When Canada’s Alimentation Couche-Tard was in talks to acquire 7-Eleven Japan last year, many local fans expressed concern about new ownership potentially tinkering with how the chain does business and damaging the quality of its products. They breathed sigh of relief when the deal didn’t go through, but there’ll likely be some trepidation from Starbucks fans in Japan if/when the coffeehouse starts being run by someone else.

According to Reuters’ report, the exact amount of stock that Starbucks Corporation would unload is still under consideration, but the company is looking to sell off at least enough to constitute a majority share, and thus control, of Starbucks Japan, and the sale process could be starting before the end of this year.

title: Get more room in your luggage with new clothing compression machines at Haneda and Narita airports
description: Forget packing hacks, Pocket Tips is the fastest and easiest way to create more room in your suitcase. When you’re travelling to Japan, every inch of space in your suitcase is precious, because after buying up all the unique Japan-only products you come across here, you might find yourself wondering if you should start discarding […]
content:
Forget packing hacks, Pocket Tips is the fastest and easiest way to create more room in your suitcase.

When you’re travelling to Japan, every inch of space in your suitcase is precious, because after buying up all the unique Japan-only products you come across here, you might find yourself wondering if you should start discarding your clothes just to make room for your souvenirs.

Even with all the packing hacks out there, it can still be near-impossible to try and fit everything into your luggage, but now Japan has come up with a solution to free up more space, and it’s called “Pocket Tips”. This new service uses an automatic compression machine to shrink clothing and create more space inside your suitcase.

▼ The machine is about the same size as an ATM.

Developed with support from Haneda, Narita, Kumamoto, and Naha airports, the machine has already been trialled at these locations, and the companies are now working towards full-scale implementation at the four airports.

The Pocket Tips machine has been praised for its ease of use – simply fold your clothes into the mould, then place it in the machine and press the button. In just around a minute, your clothes will be reduced to as little as one-seventh of their original bulk, becoming a compact little cube that packs easily into your suitcase.

The process doesn’t require plastic compression bags, and it can even be used on bulky items like towels.

The compressed clothes can be returned to their original shape by washing them or leaving them spread out for around 15 minutes.

▼ A 3L-size (roughly XXXL) T-shirt after compression

The compression service gives travellers a significant amount of extra room for souvenirs, which is exactly what they’ve been wanting. During the trial period, out of 400 people surveyed, about 70 percent said they had previously given up buying additional souvenirs because they didn’t have enough space in their luggage. After using the service, around 89 percent of participants said they would like to use it again.

▼ One happy customer

Though previous trials have mainly focused on travellers preparing to fly out of Japan, giving them room for last-minute purchases at the airport, the service is now being eyed for use in both directions, allowing travellers to compress their clothes upon arrival as well as before departure.

▼ Travellers lining up to use the machine during one of the trials

The machine has been developed by SJOY, a Tokyo-based apparel company that also develops clothing-compression technology, and terminal.0 HANEDA, a research and development facility operated by Japan Airport Terminal Co., Ltd., which manages Haneda Airport’s passenger terminals.

While an official launch date is yet to be announced, 2027 has been reported as the target for full-scale implementation. The companies are currently working to determine where the machines should be installed, how they should be operated and how safety considerations should be handled before full-scale implementation takes place. SJOY also says it’s considering future applications at places like hotels and in the apparel industry.

With so many travellers crying out for more room in their luggage, a service like this would be particularly helpful in hotels, and it couldn’t come at a better time, as Japan is welcoming more tourists than ever to its shores.

title: Everything old is new, and cool, again at this hotel in Japan’s hot spring town comeback king
description: As a new generation of travelers discovers Atami, it’s the New Akao’s time to shine again. Atami is a great town to go to if you don’t want to do anything. That’s not a sarcastic, backhanded compliment, either. The coastal town in Shizuoka Prefecture is famous for its seaside hot spring inns and hotels, and […]
content:
As a new generation of travelers discovers Atami, it’s the New Akao’s time to shine again.

Atami is a great town to go to if you don’t want to do anything. That’s not a sarcastic, backhanded compliment, either. The coastal town in Shizuoka Prefecture is famous for its seaside hot spring inns and hotels, and the quintessential Atami getaway involves lots of looking out at the ocean, soaking in hot spring baths, and looking out at the ocean while soaking in hot spring baths.

Atami had its heyday in the late Showa Era years of the 1960s, ‘70s, and ‘80s, but once the bubble economy popped, the stream of travelers largely dried up. By the time the economy had picked up again, the town had acquired a bad rap as an unfashionably outdated place to visit, Recently, though, there’s been a boom in interest in the Showa retro aesthetic, and Atami is once again a top travel destination, as our Japanese-language reporter Natsuno Futon saw first-hand on her recent visit.

The rotary area just outside Atami Station, as well as the covered shopping street that extends from it, were filled with travelers looking for tasty things to eat and souvenirs to buy (such as plushies of Atami’s balding middle-aged man fairy mascot). But like we said, one of the best things to do in Atami is “nothing,” and Natsuno was headed to one of the best places in town to do just that.

Several hotel shuttle buses make stops at the Atami Station rotary, and the one that Natsuno and her family were waiting for was the one for guests of the Hotel New Akao.

The New Akao is the Atami hotel, a major landmark that’s been known to travel fans in Japan for decades. The ride to the hotel from the station takes about 10 minutes, so it’s not far, but it feels like a trip to another world as the bus enters this tunnel along the way.

Once you come out the other end, the road continues rising and winding…

…and then the iconic, old-school New Akao (ニューアカオ) sign comes into view.

As you can see, the hotel stands very close to the water, which gives it some fantastic views…

…but the interior is no slouch either, and as soon as you step into the lobby, you’re whisked back to the old-school luxury of the Showa era.

There’s no modern minimalism here. The lobby is nicely maintained, but also unabashedly proud and committed to the now-retro aesthetic, with plush patterned carpet as far as the floorspace allows.

As Natsuno was traveling with her husband and two daughter, they’d booked a room with three beds.

As you can see, their guestroom has been renovated compared to the lobby, and the style is a nice mix of contemporary comfort and nods to Showa sensibilities in its color schemes.

And since there room was in the hotel’s Ocean Wing, the window gave them a great vantage point to see the light of the late-afternoon sun dancing on the surface of the water.

If you’re craving a bit of a sea breeze, the window does open, but just a bit, because if you were to slip or drop your phone…

…it’s a long way down.

As mentioned above, Atami was a major travel hotspot during the bubble economy, when lavish employee trips were a common part of Japanese business culture. That trend has largely died down nowadays, and the New Akao recently converted one of its private banquet rooms into a kids play park, with Natsuno’s daughter made good use of.

In addition to equipment to climb in and around, there’s a nod to the hotel’s past with a retro section with classic toys and electronics…

…and right next to it is a digital play space where kids can turn their hand-drawn illustrations into projected images.

But something that hasn’t changed is the New Akao’s main dining room, called Nishiki.

It may be a restaurant, but the vibe here is more like a grand theater, giving each meal a touch of dramatic flair.

▼ The buffet’s Mt. Fuji-shaped cakes were especially clever.

▼ If you’re lucky, your meal might even coincide with a live piano performance.

Of course, Atami is first and foremost a hot spring town, and the New Akao has several different indoor and open-air bath areas. Guest photography isn’t allowed in them, but they’re all beautiful, as these photos from the hotel’s official website show.

Actually, there’s beauty to be found all over the hotel. Because of its cliffside location, the facilities are arranged in a sort of terraced array, with hallways and staircases connecting one part of the property with another.

Some of these passages have unique and charming art displays, while others have windows that give you perspectives of the surrounding scenery you can’t get anywhere else in town, making them enticing spaces to explore.

By the way, if you like to have a few more structured activities on your travel itinerary, the New Akao does have a wealth of options, ranging from yoga classes and cycling tours to crafting classes, sea kayaking, and an “ocean pool” for adventurous swimmers.

But it’s a hotel that’s especially hard to beat if you’re in the mood to just relax, and as long as that something that travelers like to do, the New Akao will be a place for them.

title: OC Japan Fair returns to California packed with all kinds of Japanese culture

From 16 to 18 October, the OC Japan Fair will be putting food, traditional culture, pop culture, music, shopping, and more in the spotlight, giving Californians […]
content:
Tuna dismantling? You bet!

Every year, a weekend celebration of almost all things Japanese takes place in Orange County, California, and this year it’s coming back bigger than ever. From 16 to 18 October, the OC Japan Fair will be putting food, traditional culture, pop culture, music, shopping, and more in the spotlight, giving Californians a rare glimpse into many corners of life in Japan.

The main event is set to be the Japan Pop Culture Zone. This section will make up about half the entire indoor space of the venue and will showcase major anime titles, with Dan Da Dan and Blue Lock announced so far.

Also seeing some growth this year is Cosplay & Ai♡Fes Idol Festival, loaded with cosplayers and idols active in both Japan and California performing, including Sakura Graduation from Nagoya, who will be performing on all three days of the festival.

In addition to the anime and idols at OC Japan Fair, an entire Akihabara Electric Town exhibit will once again be set up to recreate the sights and sounds of the famous district in Tokyo.

On the other hand, classical Japanese culture will also be represented. In contrast to the modern Akihabara, the Asakusa district of Tokyo will also have its atmosphere recreated in the Asakusa & Nakamise Street Traditional Culture Area. Kabuki dance, rakugo comedy, taiko drums, koto music, Nihon buyo dance, shodo calligraphy, kado flower arrangement, sado tea ceremonies, kimono… The list just keeps going, and it can all be seen in one weekend.

There will also be a Bon Odori dance experience, a cornerstone of the Japanese festival experience. An Oiran Dochu procession of courtesans held centuries ago will be reenacted on Saturday and Sunday, with full Edo period costumes.

Food and shopping will both be in full effect as well. Over 60 kinds of Japanese foods, from okonomiyaki to fried pork cutlet sandwiches, will be sold alongside a vast array of Japanese goods from anime merch to traditional Japanese crafts.

Also, a very unique part of Japanese culture will be on display in the form of a Tuna Dismantling Show (Maguro Kaitai Show). Although it’s called a “Tuna Cutting Show” by OC Japan Fair, I don’t think “cutting” really does justice to the technical precision and speed that goes into these things. Often performed on auspicious occasions like the opening of fish markets or even weddings, this involves a highly skilled chef carving up an entire tuna fish with the efficiency of an F1 pit crew.

▼ And the result of a Tuna Dismantling Show

With all the additions to this year’s festival, you might expect admission to go up, but instead the organizers decided to lower the cost of entry from last year to make it more accessible. Tickets are available for as low as US$13.58 if purchased in advance before 30 September, and admission is free for everyone under 6 years old or 65 years old and over.

The time will never be more right to get a really comprehensive taste of Japan without actually coming here, so be sure to check it out this October.

title: Does Tokyo need self-driving taxis? Waymo thinks so, plans to launch fleet soon

content:
It’s hard to see why Tokyoites would prefer self-driving cabs to regular ones, but that might not be what Waymo is betting on.

Japan has, by and large, passed on ride-sharing services. Though they’ve flourished in many other parts of the world, Japan’s demographics and public transportation infrastructure is such that owning your own car is a discretionary luxury in urban and suburban communities, and so car-owners usually aren’t in income brackets where they have a strong incentive or need to make a few extra bucks as drivers. Meanwhile, there’s not much passenger demand among residents of rural Japan, where having a car of your own is pretty much a necessity on a daily basis.

The result is that Uber’s presence in Japan is far larger in the food delivery business than the people moving one. However, even if the country is largely skipping ride-sharing, Waymo still thinks it has a chance to shake up the Japanese taxi industry, and it’s looking to introduce fully self-driving cabs in Tokyo soon.

Last year, the U.S.-based Waymo entered into a strategic partnership with Japanese taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and Go, a Japanese taxi-hailing app partly owned by Nihon Kotsu. In the year since, they’ve been conducting tests of Waymo vehicles on Tokyo streets, with a Nihon Kotsu driver onboard to ensure safety and take over when needed. The three companies now feel they’re ready to start taking steps towards the next phase of their plan, launching Japan’s first fleet of fully self-driving, unmanned taxis, which they hope to have running about Tokyo’s streets sometime in 2027.

The companies say that safety will be their highest priority as they gradually introduce a growing number of self-driving taxis, with an initial goal of approximately 100 vehicles in Tokyo. Tokyo’s road network is a complex mixture of congested major thoroughfares and narrow backstreets, with a very large percentage of uncontrolled or irregularly shaped intersections, all of which make self-driving a challenge from a technical standpoint.

▼ There’s no word as to whether or not Waymo’s self-driving cars will follow the Japanese taxi norm of lace doilies on the seats.

Even if Waymo’s vehicles can learn to navigate Tokyo’s streets, though, there’s still the question of how much consumer demand there is in the city for self-driving taxis. Ostensibly, eliminating the driver would allow for lower operating costs, which could, theoretically, be passed on to consumers in the form of lower fares. However, because Tokyo  has such convenient train, subway, and bus networks, taxi travel is already seen as something of a luxury among locals and travelers. Most people who are looking for a cab aren’t particularly concerned about the price, and Waymo would probably have to offer fares that are substantially cheaper than conventional taxis’ in order to entice rail or bus users strongly enough to take a ride in their self-driving cars.

The added pickup convenience presented by self-driving cabs might also not have such significant appeal, since taxi usage in Tokyo tends to be either between two downtown locations or, if the trains have already stopped running for the night, from downtown back to the suburbs. In either case, the rides are starting in a developed location, where it’s usually not hard to find a taxi on the street. By comparison, calling a taxi to come pick you up at your home in the suburbs is a far less common scenario.

All that said, it is true that Japan’s professional driver workforce, including taxi drivers, has been steadily growing older, with fewer new drivers coming into the industry than veteran drivers retiring. As such, Waymo and Nihon Kotsu might not be looking to launch driverless taxis because they think customers will prefer them to conventional cabs, but as preparation for an expected coming labor shortage that could make it difficult to find and hire enough human drivers. If/when that happens, there’s bound to be a portion of the population that still feels uneasy riding in a self-driving car, but if they have to, they’d probably rather ride in one from a provider that isn’t a complete newcomer to the market, so Waymo’s starting fleet in Tokyo is probably more about trying to build trust and recognition than making a quick profit.
